1219.title: They are his
1219.hook: Ravana's own brother asks Rama for refuge, and the bhakti sutras end on why no devotee is ranked
1219.carry: bhakti has no ranks: all who love are his
1219.tomorrow: a king with everything asks to become one thing. what?
1219.howItsDone: In devotional Hindu communities, the closing sutras are read as a portrait of the ideal devotee, and the forms of love they list, such as servant, friend, parent and beloved, are familiar ways of relating to God in bhakti traditions.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-NINETEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti as a taste that can't be told, like a taste for someone who cannot speak, growing every moment.
screen: `A TASTE THAT CAN'T BE TOLD.`

segments.voice: On the shore across from Lanka, Rama's army watches a stranger come through the sky with four companions: Vibhishana, the demon king Ravana's own brother. He begged Ravana to give Sita back, was thrown out for it, and has come with nothing to offer but himself. Sugriva and others want him seized. Wrong family, wrong side, maybe a spy. Rama says no. In Valmiki's Ramayana he makes a vow: whoever comes to me even once, saying I am yours, I give safety from every being.
screen: `A STRANGER FROM LANKA.` → `WRONG FAMILY, WRONG SIDE.` → `I AM YOURS.`

segments.voice: The Narada Bhakti Sutras, which we finish today, name Vibhishana in their last pages among the teachers of love, next to Vyasa and Hanuman. Ravana's brother, listed as a master. That fits what the sutras say about the people of bhakti. When they talk together about the Lord, their throats choke, the hair on their arms stands up, and tears come. They make the holy places holier. And among them, the sutras say, there is no distinction of birth, learning, looks, family, wealth or work. Why? Tadiyah. Because they are his. That's one of Hinduism's big teachings, said plainly: in bhakti, belonging to God outranks everything else on the list. Family, degree, bank account: none of it sets your place. Rama on the shore is that line acted out. Then some advice. Don't lean on argument; it settles nothing. Read the books of love and do what wakes it up. Keep the plain virtues: not harming, truthfulness, purity, compassion, faith. And love, though one, takes eleven forms, among them love as a servant, a friend, a parent, a beloved, love that remembers, and the ache of being apart. Many teachers read that list as bhakti letting people come to God as they are. The book closes with a promise said twice: whoever trusts this teaching becomes a devotee and reaches the most beloved. Most of us rank people quietly, by school, job or family. The sutras say that in the house of love, those ladders aren't there.
screen: `RAVANA'S BROTHER, AMONG THE TEACHERS.` · `NO DISTINCTION: THEY ARE HIS.` · `ONE LOVE, ELEVEN FORMS.` · then, large: `BHAKTI HAS NO RANKS.`

segments.voice: Let the sutras' forms of love drift past slowly: a servant's, glad to help; a friend's; a parent's, watching over; a beloved's; love that remembers; love that aches when apart. Don't choose; notice which one warms a little as it passes, toward God if you pray, or toward a person you love if not, and stay with that one. Then, if you pray, say once the words Vibhishana brought to Rama: i am yours. If you don't, just stay with that person in mind.
Bhakti. In the last pages of the sutras, one love in eleven forms, and its people, among whom there is no distinction, because they are his.

1220.title: The king who asked to be a step
1220.hook: a king's wish list: a fish in the temple pond, a tree on the hill, a step at the shrine's door
1220.carry: dasya: a servant's love, always facing god
1220.tomorrow: a singer kept outside the temple. who carries him in?
1220.howItsDone: In Sri Vaishnava worship, the Alvars' Tamil hymns are recited in temples and homes, and pilgrims at Tirupati are told of Kulasekhara Alvar's wish to be a step before the Lord.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-TWENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday finished the Narada Bhakti Sutras: one love in eleven forms, and no distinction among its people, because they are his.
screen: `ONE LOVE, ELEVEN FORMS.` · `THEY ARE HIS.`

segments.voice: A king sits down to write a wish list. He already has the throne, the palace, the army. So what does he wish for? To be a fish in a temple pond. A bird by the water. A flowering tree on a hill. And finally, a stone step at the door of a shrine, the kind people walk on without looking down. That king, in Sri Vaishnava tradition, is Kulasekhara, one of the Alvars, and the wish list is one of his hymns.
screen: `A KING'S WISH LIST.` → `A FISH, A BIRD, A TREE.` → `A STEP AT THE SHRINE'S DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, the Alvar hymns. The Alvars were poet-saints of Vishnu who sang in Tamil, and the tradition explains their name as people sunk deep in God. Now Kulasekhara. Tradition remembers him as a king of the Chera country, on India's southwest coast, who loved the Lord more than his crown. His hymns are gathered as the Perumal Tirumozhi, the holy words of the king. In one set of verses he turns toward Venkatam, the sacred hill of Vishnu, and makes his wishes. Something small on that hill: a bird by the pond, a fish in its water, a servant who carries things for the Lord, a tree that flowers there. And then the image that stayed. Let me lie as a step, he sings, so I can see your coral mouth. Stood on by everyone who comes, low and still, but always facing the Lord. The tradition says the threshold step of the shrine at Tirupati, on that hill, carries his name to this day: Kulasekharan padi, Kulasekhara's step. The verses end with something like: let me be anything at all on that hill. Notice what the king gives up: not just wealth, but height. Hindu bhakti has a name for this love: dasya, a servant's love, one of the forms the Narada sutras listed yesterday. The servant's place is low, but it's the one that always faces the Lord. So the one who sets out the chairs at the puja, or stands at the back, isn't lower here. In the king's hymn, that's the clearest view.
screen: `POET-SAINTS OF VISHNU, IN TAMIL.` · `KULASEKHARA, A KING WHO SANG.` · `LET ME LIE AS A STEP.` · then, large: `DASYA: A SERVANT'S LOVE.`

segments.voice: Let your gaze drop to the floor a little way in front of you, the height a step would see from, and let thoughts of rank, titles, who's ahead, what you're owed, pass over you like footsteps. Then lift your eyes just a little, toward a picture, a window or the open space ahead, and keep that one direction, the way the step keeps facing the shrine. If you pray, you can face God this way, from the threshold.
The Alvar hymns. Tamil songs to Vishnu by poet-saints the tradition calls sunk deep in God, like Kulasekhara, the king who asked to be a step.

segments.voice: Your line: dasya, a servant's love, always facing God. The lowest place can have the clearest view. I'll be here tomorrow.

1221.title: Carried in on a priest's shoulders
1221.hook: a singer carried into the temple looks at the Lord from the feet up
1221.carry: start at the feet: god's feet are refuge
1221.tomorrow: a month with no ghee, no milk. what do the girls lean on?
1221.howItsDone: In Sri Vaishnava tradition, Tiruppan Alvar's Amalanadipiran is recited in daily worship, and devotees are taught to behold the deity in the temple from the feet upward.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-TWENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday opened dasya, a servant's love always facing God: Kulasekhara, the king who asked to be a step at the shrine's door, low and still, facing the Lord.
screen: `LET ME LIE AS A STEP.`

segments.voice: Feet first. In the old custom of greeting an elder by touching their feet, the hand reaches down before the eyes ever meet. One Alvar's hymn runs on that same instinct. Tradition says its singer, Tiruppan, came from a community of bards kept outside the temple at Srirangam, and sang to the Lord from the riverbank. And it says a priest, Lokasaranga, was told by the Lord himself to carry the singer inside on his own shoulders. He did.
screen: `FEET BEFORE FACE.` → `A SINGER KEPT OUTSIDE.` → `CARRIED IN ON A PRIEST'S SHOULDERS.`

segments.voice: The hymn is short, named by its opening words, Amalanadipiran: the spotless one, the first Lord. What's remarkable is its path. Tiruppan stands before the image of Vishnu reclining at Srirangam, and he doesn't take it all in at once. He looks the way a devotee bows, starting at the feet. The holy feet, he sings, have come into my eyes. That's no quirk. In Sri Vaishnava prayer the Lord's feet are the refuge itself: the dvaya, one of the tradition's holiest prayers, takes refuge at Narayana's feet. It's also why Hindus touch an elder's feet: you begin low, and ask blessing there. Then his gaze rises, one verse at a time. The red cloth at the waist. The navel, where the lotus of Brahma grows. The chest, where the goddess Lakshmi dwells. The throat. The red mouth. The long, wide eyes. And then the whole dark, beautiful form at once. Each part reminds him of a story, like the throat that once swallowed the worlds. Then the last verse turns, and it's the line people remember. Having seen my nectar, he says, these eyes of mine will not look at anything else. The tradition says that with this song he merged into the Lord. Notice who sings it. A man kept outside the walls is carried in, and sings the hymn the temple keeps. Two days ago the Narada Bhakti Sutras said there is no distinction among those who love, because they are his. Here, on a priest's shoulders, is that line acted out.
screen: `AMALANADIPIRAN: THE SPOTLESS ONE.` · `THE GAZE BEGINS AT THE FEET.` · `THE FEET ARE THE REFUGE.` · `THESE EYES WON'T LOOK ELSEWHERE.`

segments.voice: Choose something in front of you, an image you hold sacred if you have one, or a plant, or a face in a photo, and look only at the bottom of it for a breath or two. Then let the eyes rise a little at a time, staying with each part, and only at the top take it all in at once and rest there. If you pray, you can let this be a way of beholding God.
The Alvar hymns. In Tiruppan's Amalanadipiran, a gaze that rises from the Lord's feet to his eyes and then won't look at anything else.

1222.title: Andal's dawn vow
1222.hook: a list of things a group of girls won't do for a month, and what they lean on when they finally reach Krishna's door
1222.carry: keep the vow, but lean on grace, not merit
1222.tomorrow: three strangers, one tiny shelter, rain. who's the fourth?
1222.howItsDone: In the month of Margazhi, Sri Vaishnava temples and households recite Andal's Tiruppavai before dawn, and teachers explain its verses on the rules of the vow and on the bond with the Lord that can't be undone.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-TWENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: start at the feet, God's feet are refuge. Tiruppan was carried into the temple and looked at the Lord from the feet up, one part at a time.
screen: `FROM THE FEET UP.` · `TODAY: THE RULES OF A VOW.`

segments.voice: No ghee. No milk. A bath before dawn. No kohl on the eyes, no flowers in the hair. That's part of a list, kept by the girls of Krishna's cowherd village as they set out on a vow for the month of Margazhi. The list is a hymn. Andal, one of the Alvars, sang it in her Tiruppavai, the song of the dawn vow. Year three walked with those girls as they woke each other in the dark and went knocking at Krishna's door. Today, two other pages of the same song: the rules they keep on the way, and what they say about themselves when they arrive.
screen: `NO GHEE. NO MILK.` → `NO KOHL, NO FLOWERS.` → `ANDAL'S TIRUPPAVAI.`

segments.voice: Early in the hymn, the girls set out the vow. They'll bathe before dawn. They'll go without ghee and milk. They won't line their eyes or put flowers in their hair. They won't do what shouldn't be done, and they won't go carrying harmful words about anyone. Then the list turns from giving up to giving: alms and gifts, as much as they're able. So the vow trims the comforts, guards the tongue, and opens the hand. At the end of the hymn, they finally stand before Krishna. They don't mention the cold baths or the missed ghee. We follow the cows into the woods and eat there, they say. We're a cowherd clan with no learning at all. Our one good fortune is that you were born among us. Then the line Sri Vaishnava teachers keep coming back to: the bond between you and us can't be undone here, even if someone tried. We're children who don't know any better, they add; if, out of love, we called you by small names, don't be angry. A month of discipline, and at the door they don't hold it up. Sri Vaishnava teachers read a big teaching here: you don't reach God by stacking up merit. You're held by the relationship, and by grace. Keep the vow; it gets you out of bed in the dark and shapes you. Just don't bring it to the door as a bill.
screen: `BATHE BEFORE DAWN. NO GHEE, NO MILK.` · `NO HARMFUL WORDS. GIVE WHAT YOU CAN.` · `THE BOND CAN'T BE UNDONE.` · then, large: `GRACE, NOT MERIT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you're close to, or God if you pray, and notice any urge to arrive with a list: what you've done for them, how hard you've tried, what you've given up. Let the list go quiet, one item at a time, and rest in the plain fact of the bond, with nothing to show. If a small, fond name for them comes to mind, let it come.

1223.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas tell the story of the three Alvars at Tirukkovalur, and their three linked hymns are recited as part of the collection of Alvar songs in temples and homes.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-TWENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: keep the vow, but lean on grace, not merit. Andal's girls kept a vow of small renunciations, and at Krishna's door leaned only on the bond.
screen: `THE BOND AT THE DOOR.` · `TODAY: A LAMP IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Rain, hard and sudden, at night, in a town called Tirukkovalur. A wandering singer ducks into a tiny covered passage, room enough for one to lie down. A second soaked stranger asks to come in. Room for one to lie, the first says, means room for two to sit. A third arrives. Room for two to sit means room for three to stand. So three strangers stand shoulder to shoulder in the dark, dripping. Then the space gets tighter, as if a fourth body has pressed in among them. Nobody came through the door. That's the story the Sri Vaishnava tradition tells about how three of the Alvar hymns began.
screen: `RAIN, AND ROOM FOR ONE.` → `TWO SIT. THREE STAND.` → `A FOURTH PRESSES IN.`

segments.voice: The three, the story goes, were Poygai, Bhutam and Pey. Crammed in the dark with someone unseen, they don't panic or push. Each one lights a lamp, and the lamps are songs. Poygai sings a lamp on the scale of the world: the earth for the bowl, the ocean for the oil, the blazing sun for the flame, offered at the feet of the Lord. Bhutam answers with a lamp on the scale of a heart: love for the bowl, longing for the oil, a mind melting with joy for the wick, lit as a lamp of knowing. In that double light, Pey sings what he sees. The fourth one, pressing in, is Vishnu, with Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune, beside him. I have seen, he sings, and he names it: the goddess, a golden form, a color like the blazing sun, the wheel, the conch. Sri Vaishnavas read the story as God wanting to be among his devotees, standing there the whole time. And it shows why a lamp comes first in so much Hindu worship. Many families light a diya at dusk; at the aarti a flame is waved before the deity. The lamp is an offering, and it's how you see who's there: one lamp outside, one of love inside. Each Alvar's verses became a linked hymn, an antadi.
screen: `THREE ALVARS, ONE DARK SHELTER.` · `A LAMP AS BIG AS THE WORLD.` · `A LAMP MADE OF LOVE.` · then, large: `LIGHT THE LAMP. GOD IS NEAR.`

segments.voice: Light two lamps. First the wide one: let your attention open to everything at once, the floor holding you, the air, the sky above the roof. Then the close one: bring to mind someone or something you love, and let that warmth fill the chest like oil in a small bowl. Sit in both kinds of light and see who seems near; if you pray, let the one you pray to be the one who's near.
The Alvar hymns. Today, three singers in one dark shelter, two lamps, and a fourth who was already there.

1224.title: Many years to God
1224.hook: God appears in the sky over a city, and the old devotee's first worry is that someone might put the evil eye on him
1224.carry: vatsalya: loving god like your own child
1224.tomorrow: ten verses say they're part of a thousand. where's the rest?
1224.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas sing Periyalvar's Tiruppallandu in their temples and homes as a blessing over the Lord, alongside Periyalvar's songs of Yashoda and the child Krishna.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-TWENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: light the lamp, and God is already near. Three strangers in the rain lit a lamp as big as the world and a lamp made of love, and found Vishnu standing among them.
screen: `TWO LAMPS IN THE DARK.` · `TODAY: A BLESSING FOR GOD.`

segments.voice: A grandmother sees a beautiful baby in the street and, before anything else, says a quick word against the evil eye. Too much praise, the old worry goes, and something bad might follow. Now move that instinct. The Sri Vaishnava tradition tells of a temple garland-maker named Vishnuchitta who, on a day of great honor, looked up and saw Vishnu himself in the sky, riding the eagle Garuda, come to watch. Crowds everywhere. The old man's first feeling wasn't awe, or a request. It was worry: someone might cast the evil eye on him. So he did what that grandmother does. He sang a blessing over God.
screen: `A WORD AGAINST THE EVIL EYE.` → `VISHNU IN THE SKY.` → `THE OLD MAN WORRIES FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: The blessing is the Tiruppallandu, and its key word is pallandu, many years. Many years, many years, the song begins, to your holy feet. Then the blessing spreads: many years to the goddess at your side, to the wheel and to the conch. It's what you sing over a child or an elder you love, and here it's sung to the Lord of the universe. Tradition says that's why Vishnuchitta came to be called Periyalvar, the great Alvar. Tradition says he also found and raised Andal, whose dawn vow came two days ago, so a father and a daughter both sit among the Alvars. His longer hymns keep the same tenderness. In them he sings as Yashoda, Krishna's foster mother: rocking the cradle, coaxing the toddler to come for his bath, calling the moon down to play with him. God as a little one who needs looking after. Hindu teachers have a word for this kind of love: vatsalya, a parent's love, given back to God. It's why many Hindu homes care for a small image of baby Krishna: bathing him, feeding him, singing him to sleep. A prayer can bring God a need. Periyalvar brings God his care. Love, in these hymns, isn't only being protected; it's wanting to protect.
screen: `PALLANDU: MANY YEARS.` · `A BLESSING SUNG OVER GOD.` · `SINGING AS YASHODA.` · then, large: `VATSALYA: A PARENT'S LOVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love and see them clearly, their face, their hands. Instead of wanting anything from them, wish them long life, many years, many years, letting the wish travel out with each breath. If another person comes to mind, bless them too; if you pray, let the blessing rise toward the name you pray to, the way Periyalvar did.
The Alvar hymns. Today, Periyalvar's many years: a blessing sung over God, and the love of a parent given back to the divine.

1225.title: The Tamil Veda comes home
1225.hook: pilgrims sing ten verses that say they're part of a thousand, and a teacher sets out to find the rest
1225.carry: the tamil veda: holy words in the people's tongue
1225.tomorrow: a dead teacher's fingers curl tight. what promise opens them?
1225.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas chant Nammalvar's Tiruvaymoli in temples and homes alongside the Sanskrit Veda, and remember Nathamuni as the teacher who recovered the hymns.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-TWENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was vatsalya, loving God like your own child. Periyalvar looked up at God and sang a blessing over him: many years.
screen: `MANY YEARS.` · `TODAY: TEN VERSES, AND A THOUSAND.`

segments.voice: Ten verses, sung by pilgrims at the temple in Kumbakonam. A teacher named Nathamuni hears them and is moved. Then he hears the last verse say these ten are part of a thousand. A thousand? He asks the pilgrims for the rest. They don't have them. He asks everywhere. Nobody does. That, the Sri Vaishnava tradition says, is how a lost Tamil scripture began to come home. Year three met its singer, Nammalvar, the silent boy under the tamarind who answered a riddle. Today, how his songs were nearly lost, and found.
screen: `TEN VERSES AT KUMBAKONAM.` → `TEN OUT OF A THOUSAND?` → `NOBODY HAS THE REST.`

segments.voice: So Nathamuni goes to Tirukkurugur, Nammalvar's town, to the tamarind where the silent boy once sat. Nobody there has the thousand either. But, tradition says, someone gives him a short hymn: the one Madhurakavi, Nammalvar's disciple, sang in praise of his teacher. Recite this, he's told. He does, over and over, until Nammalvar appears to him and gives back the hymns. Nathamuni sets them to music and teaches them, and his line of teachers would later reach Ramanuja. The key wasn't a library, but a disciple's song of love for his teacher. What came back is the Tiruvaymoli, longing set to verse. Sometimes Nammalvar sings as himself. Sometimes he sings as a girl missing her beloved, sending birds as messengers to Vishnu. And sometimes the joy is so full that God and the singer seem to have swallowed each other. Tradition calls this song the Tamil Veda. That's a big claim, said plainly: for Sri Vaishnavas, scripture isn't only Sanskrit. A saint's song in the language people spoke at home is Veda too, and they speak of two Vedantas, Sanskrit and Tamil, read together.
screen: `TO THE TAMARIND AT TIRUKKURUGUR.` · `A DISCIPLE'S SHORT HYMN.` · `THE SONGS GIVEN BACK.` · then, large: `THE TAMIL VEDA.`

segments.voice: Walk back through the Alvar days, one breath for each: the king who asked to be a step, Tiruppan's slow look from the feet up, Andal's girls at the door, three lamps in the rain, Periyalvar's many years, and ten verses that led to a thousand. Don't weigh them; notice which one stays a moment longer, and rest there. If you pray, you can offer that moment to God.
The Alvar hymns. Today, Nammalvar's Tiruvaymoli, lost and found again through a disciple's small hymn, which the tradition calls the Tamil Veda.
screen: `THE ALVAR HYMNS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Tamil Veda, holy words in the people's tongue. One small hymn sung again and again, and a thousand came home. Until tomorrow.
